semantic_correction.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes says that several traditional foods are central to family meals and worries that diabetes care will require giving them up completely. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Incorporate the client’s usual and culturally important foods into an individualized eating plan that also meets metabolic and nutrition goals.
options.B: Begin with a standardized diabetes meal plan and add traditional foods after glucose targets improve, so cultural preferences do not complicate early teaching.
options.C: Focus the meal plan mainly on carbohydrate totals and portion sizes, then address cultural food preferences later if the client has difficulty following it.
options.D: Recommend a Mediterranean-style meal plan as the starting pattern and replace the client’s traditional foods until the care team confirms stable glycemic control.

semantic_correction.rationale: The 2026 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care emphasize that there is no one-size-fits-all eating pattern for people with diabetes and that meal planning should be individualized. Eating plans are based on the person's usual eating style, cultural background, social determinants of health, food preferences, and metabolic goals. ADA nutrition goals also include addressing individual nutrition needs based on personal and cultural preferences and maintaining the pleasure of eating through nonjudgmental messages. Recommendation 5.10 supports individualized medical nutrition therapy from a registered dietitian nutritionist, and Recommendation 5.13 supports individualized meal plans that consider nutrient quality, total calories, and metabolic goals. Therefore A is the most appropriate response. B delays integration of culturally important foods without evidence that a standardized plan must come first. C gives carbohydrate totals disproportionate priority and postpones an important part of person-centered planning. D incorrectly treats one evidence-based eating pattern as a required starting pattern and unnecessarily excludes familiar foods.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Provide culturally responsive diabetes nutrition education by incorporating the client’s usual foods and preferences into an individualized eating plan that supports metabolic and nutrition goals, with individualized MNT/RDN support as appropriate.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
semantic_correction.source_document_title: 5. Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Diabetes Care 2026;49(Supplement 1):S89–S124; published December 8, 2025; primary article rechecked August 20, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Recommendation 5.5: culturally and socially appropriate DSMES responsive to personal preferences and needs. Medical Nutrition Therapy section: no one-size-fits-all eating pattern and collaborative individualized eating plan. Recommendation 5.10: individualized MNT by an RDN. Recommendation 5.13: individualized meal plans considering nutrient quality, calories, and metabolic goals. Eating Patterns and Meal Planning: eating plans are based on usual eating style, cultural background, SDOH, and food preferences; macronutrient distribution is individualized to eating patterns, preferences, and metabolic goals. Nutrition Therapy Goals: address personal and cultural preferences and maintain pleasure of eating with nonjudgmental messages.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current ADA guidance supports culturally responsive, individualized diabetes nutrition planning based on usual eating patterns, personal and cultural preferences, and metabolic goals rather than requiring a standardized meal plan or abandonment of traditional foods.
semantic_correction.blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p.9 (official PDF pageno 12): assess client readiness to learn, learning preferences and barriers to learning; provide care and education for adult clients; assess and educate clients about health risks. Detailed Health Promotion/Disease Prevention, printed p.28 (official PDF pageno 31): assess readiness to learn, learning preferences and barriers; educate clients on actions to promote and maintain health; provide follow-up; evaluate client understanding of health-promotion behaviors/activities.
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — individualized culturally responsive diabetes nutrition education
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the culturally responsive diabetes-nutrition construct, removed the original all/only distractor pattern, rebuilt the alternatives as plausible competing nutrition approaches, and made the correct response shorter than all distractors while preserving ADA person-centered nutrition guidance.

scope_exclusions.specific_foods: The item does not label any named traditional food as healthy or unhealthy and does not prescribe a particular cuisine.
scope_exclusions.macronutrient_target: No fixed carbohydrate, protein, fat, calorie, or sodium target is tested.
scope_exclusions.mediterranean_pattern: Mediterranean-style eating can be evidence-based and appropriate for some people; D is incorrect because it is imposed as a required replacement for the client's familiar foods rather than individualized.
scope_exclusions.RDN_scope: The nurse reinforces person-centered nutrition principles and appropriate referral; the item does not assign the nurse the full scope of individualized MNT that belongs to an RDN.
scope_exclusions.glycemic_target: No A1C or glucose target is required to answer the item.
scope_exclusions.food_access: Food access and SDOH are important components of individualized planning but are not separately tested in this stem.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘cultural food preferences individualized eating plan diabetes RDN no one size fits all’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It preserves culturally important foods within an individualized plan while still requiring nutrition and metabolic goals to be met.
option_audit.B: Plausible because standardized plans can simplify early teaching, but ADA guidance does not require delaying cultural adaptation until glycemic targets improve.
option_audit.C: Plausible because carbohydrate amount and portions matter in diabetes nutrition, but they do not justify postponing personal and cultural preferences in individualized planning.
option_audit.D: Plausible because Mediterranean-style patterns are evidence-based options, but no single pattern is required and familiar foods need not be replaced wholesale.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone directly reflects individualized, culturally responsive planning. B postpones personalization, C treats preferences as secondary until adherence problems occur, and D imposes one eating pattern rather than collaboratively individualizing the plan.

cueing_check.note: The key is the shortest option; all four are complete nutrition-teaching responses with comparable detail and no all/only/always/never/every cueing.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN explicitly includes adult client education, assessment of learning preferences/barriers, health-promotion teaching, and evaluation of understanding, supporting an entry-level RN education construct that respects individual preferences.
